slides.0.title: Course Introduction
slides.0.content:
The Loire Valley is not only the kingdom of white wine — its reds and rosés have their own distinctive world. Cabernet Franc is the acknowledged 'king of Loire reds', while Gamay, Côt (Malbec), Pinot Noir and native Pineau d'Aunis complete a fascinating cast. Loire reds are celebrated for their freshness, elegant red-fruit character and outstanding food-pairing versatility.

Learning Objectives

🍷 Understand the character of Cabernet Franc

Why is Loire Cabernet Franc different from Bordeaux? What makes Chinon and Bourgueil world-class?

🌿 Meet Gamay and Côt (Malbec)

The freshness of Gamay and the structure of Côt — two complementary Loire reds

🌶️ Discover Pineau d'Aunis

The rarest and most characterful native variety — a white-pepper spice bomb

🍽️ Master food pairing for Loire reds

Light, fresh, slightly chilled — the Loire red's guide to perfect pairing
slides.1.title: Cabernet Franc: King of Loire Reds
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Elegant Red-Fruit Freshness
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Loire Cabernet Franc has higher acidity and finer tannins than Bordeaux; red fruit (raspberry, redcurrant) and violet aromas with a silky mineral finish
slides.1.highlights.1.title: The Herbal Aroma Misconception
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Green, herbaceous notes in Cabernet Franc usually indicate underripeness; top Loire producers time harvest to achieve ripe fruit while retaining freshness
slides.1.content:
While Cabernet Franc plays a supporting role to Merlot in Bordeaux, in the Loire it is the undisputed star — producing some of France's most elegant, food-friendly reds.

🏆 Premier Loire Cabernet Franc Appellations

🏰 Chinon

Location: Vienne valley, Indre-et-Loire département, around the château town of Chinon

Soils: Tuffeau plateau (structured, long ageing) + gravel terraces (supple, early drinking) + clay-sand (fresh)

Style: Dark garnet, raspberry and redcurrant aromas, violet, fine tannins, mineral finish — the most versatile of the three

Best producers: Charles Joguet, Domaine Bernard Baudry

🌿 Bourgueil / Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil

Location: North bank of the Loire, between Tours and Saumur

Soils: Sand-gravel (Saint-Nicolas — lighter, easier drinking) + tuffeau plateau (Bourgueil — structured, ages 10–15 years)

Style: Bright red fruit, lighter bodied, often recommended to serve slightly chilled at 12–14°C

💎 Saumur-Champigny

Location: South of Saumur, on tuffeau-rich plateau

Soils: Pure tuffeau

Style: Silky, refined raspberry, light mineral character — Loire red's 'ambassador'
slides.1.quiz.question: What is the key stylistic difference between Loire Cabernet Franc and Bordeaux Cabernet Franc?
slides.1.quiz.options.0: Loire Cab Franc is richer, with dark fruit and chocolate flavours
slides.1.quiz.options.1: Loire Cab Franc is fresher and more refined — red fruit and mineral character, finer tannins
slides.1.quiz.options.2: Bordeaux Cab Franc has higher acidity
slides.1.quiz.options.3: There is almost no stylistic difference between the two
slides.1.quiz.explanation: In Bordeaux, Cabernet Franc is typically blended with Merlot (and Cabernet Sauvignon), adding complexity and elegance. In the Loire, as a single variety in a cooler climate, it expresses a purer, fresher character: red fruit, violet, fine tannins and silky minerality. It is lighter and more elegant than Bordeaux but equally capable of serious ageing.
slides.2.title: Gamay and Côt (Malbec)
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Gamay: Spokesman for Fresh Fruit
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Gamay in the Loire has a distinctly different character from Beaujolais — less carbonic maceration, more genuine freshness, red fruit and mineral expression
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Côt = Malbec: The Loire's Deep-Coloured Structure
slides.2.highlights.1.content: While Malbec in Argentina is known for dark fruit and concentration, Touraine Côt retains Loire-style freshness — deeper-coloured and more structured than Cab Franc, but never heavy
slides.2.content:
In addition to Cabernet Franc, the Loire harbours two other important red varieties, each contributing a different dimension to the region's red wine palette.

🍇 Gamay in the Loire

Main AOPs: Touraine (Touraine-Amboise, Touraine-Mesland), Anjou-Gamay, Cheverny, Coteaux du Giennois

Style differences from Beaujolais:

  • Loire Gamay is usually fermented in an open-top vessel or aged briefly; carbonic maceration is less common
  • Higher acidity, stronger mineral character; more restrained fruit expression
  • Often blended with Cabernet Franc to add freshness and colour

Food pairing: Charcuterie, grilled chicken, lentil dishes; serve lightly chilled at 13–15°C

🍷 Côt (Malbec) in the Loire

History: Côt (Malbec's French name) is one of France's oldest red varieties; it was actually better established in the Loire before Cahors (and much earlier than Argentina)

Key appellation: Touraine-Amboise — the only AOP in the world requiring 100% Côt for red wine

Style: Deep purple-ruby, plum, blackberry, hint of violet; fuller-bodied than Cab Franc but retains Loire freshness; ages well (5–10 years)

Food pairing: Venison, duck confit, stewed lamb
slides.2.quiz.question: Which Loire AOP is the only one in the world requiring 100% Côt (Malbec) for red wine?
slides.2.quiz.explanation: Touraine-Amboise is the world's only AOP that mandates 100% Côt (Malbec) for red wine production. This distinction makes Touraine-Amboise a fascinating study of Malbec's Loire expression — structured but fresher and less concentrated than Cahors or Argentinian examples.
slides.3.title: Pineau d'Aunis: Native Spice
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Pepper and Wild Flower Aromas
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Pineau d'Aunis is the Loire's most aromatic native red variety — white and black pepper spices interwoven with red fruit and wild flowers are its calling card
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Revived After Near Extinction
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Once nearly abandoned, Pineau d'Aunis was saved by a handful of dedicated small producers; today it is experiencing a global natural wine renaissance
slides.3.content:
Pineau d'Aunis is one of the Loire's most fascinating native varieties — with extremely ancient origins (mentioned in records as early as the 11th century) and an utterly distinctive aromatic profile that is unlike any other grape in France.

🔍 Variety Profile

History

One of the Loire's oldest native varieties; nearly disappeared in the 20th century as it was replaced by Cabernet Franc and Gamay

Revival

Since the 1990s, a small group of natural wine producers in the Vallée du Loir and Touraine has dedicated themselves to reviving this near-lost variety

Growing Conditions

Tuffeau and clay soils; ripens late; some vintages retain higher acidity

👃 Aromatic Profile

  • Signature: White and black pepper — distinctly reminiscent of Northern Rhône Syrah, but much lighter in body
  • Red fruit: Wild strawberry, raspberry, redcurrant
  • Floral: Violet, wild rose
  • Structure: Very light body, low tannins, high freshness; sometimes made as rosé or pétillant naturel

🗺️ Key AOPs

  • Coteaux du Loir (red/rosé)
  • Touraine (varietal wine, rare)
  • Côteaux du Vendômois (red/rosé)
slides.3.quiz.question: What is the most iconic aromatic character of Pineau d'Aunis?
slides.3.quiz.options.1: White pepper spice with red fruit and floral notes
slides.3.quiz.explanation: Pineau d'Aunis' most distinctive feature is its intense pepper spice — particularly white pepper — combined with red fruit (wild strawberry, raspberry) and floral notes (violet, wild rose). This peppery quality makes it the closest Loire parallel to Northern Rhône Syrah, though far lighter in body.
slides.4.title: Red Varieties & Food Pairing at a Glance
slides.4.highlights.0.title: The Light-Bodied Philosophy of Loire Reds
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Loire reds are not rivals to Bordeaux or Burgundy in power — they offer elegance, freshness and extraordinary food-pairing versatility
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Serve Slightly Chilled for Best Results
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Many Loire reds are recommended at 12–14°C — slightly cooler than the typical red wine serving temperature — to highlight their fresh fruit and mineral character
slides.4.content:
Loire reds represent a completely different philosophy of red wine — not power, but precision; not extraction, but expression. Understanding this is the key to both appreciating and recommending them.

🍽️ Loire Red Food Pairing Guide

Variety / AOPStyleIdeal PairingsServing Temp.
Chinon (tuffeau)Structured, mineral, ageableRoasted duck, mushroom risotto, aged cheese14–16°C
Chinon (gravel)Fresh, supple, early drinkingRabbit rillettes, charcuterie13–15°C
Bourgueil / Saint-NicolasLight, fresh red fruitCold cuts, grilled salmon, light pasta12–14°C
Saumur-ChampignySilky, elegant, mineralVeal, light poultry, Loire fish (pike-perch)13–15°C
Touraine-Amboise (Côt)Medium-full, plummyDuck confit, braised lamb, venison14–16°C
Gamay LoireLight, fresh fruitCharcuterie, grilled chicken, lentils12–14°C
Pineau d'AunisUltra-light, pepperyGoat's cheese, light fish, tapas11–13°C

❄️ Why Serve Loire Reds Chilled?

Most Loire reds have relatively light bodies and high freshness (acidity). Serving them at 12–14°C — slightly cooler than classic red wine temperature — highlights their fresh fruit and mineral character, and prevents the wine from tasting flat or heavy. This is not unusual practice: in the Loire region itself, many producers and restaurants serve reds this way.
slides.4.quiz.question: Why are many Loire reds (such as Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil) recommended to be served at 12–14°C?
slides.4.quiz.options.0: The residual sugar is enhanced at lower temperatures
slides.4.quiz.options.1: Lower temperature highlights their fresh fruit and acidity, perfectly matching the Loire's light style
slides.4.quiz.options.2: They are sensitive to room temperature and would oxidise
slides.4.quiz.options.3: It is a Loire Valley tradition with no particular technical reason
slides.4.quiz.explanation: Loire reds are built on freshness and light to medium body. Serving them at 12–14°C (rather than the 16–18°C typical for heavier reds) keeps the fresh fruit and mineral character vibrant, and prevents the wine feeling flabby or over-warm. This is particularly important for varieties like Gamay and Cabernet Franc in their lighter manifestations.
